all_quotes.quote: the mass accretion rate is estimated to be quite low as < 2 \times 10^{-8} M_{\odot} yr^{-1} with the assumption of a stellar radius of 1.5 R_{\odot}.
We have clearly detected the blueshifted and redshifted emission of the ^{12}CO (J = 3–2) at MMS-1 (Figure 1 (a,b)) for the first time at the present high-angular resolution.
It is to be noted that we cannot detect high-density tracers, H^{13}CO^{+} (J = 3–2) and C^{17}O (J = 3–2), toward MMS-1 even with the higher angular resolution compared with Paper II.

all_quotes.loc: A detached disk at the center of an isolated protostellar core
all_quotes.quote: The observed disk in MMS-1 is very small, indicating that further significant mass accretion through the disk does not occur anymore. Thus, we may be witnessing a stage close to the moment when the accretion activity has been halting.
The spatial/velocity distributions of the gas show there is a rotating disk with a size scale of ~10 AU, a disk mass of ~10^{-4} M_{\odot} and a central stellar mass of ~0.2 M_{\odot}.

It is to be noted that we cannot detect high-density tracers, H^{13}CO^{+} (J = 3–2) and C^{17}O (J = 3–2), toward MMS-1 even with the higher angular resolution compared with Paper II. These results indicate that the disk may be detached from the surrounding environment although it is located at the center of the dense core whose density is ~10^6 cm^{-3}.

However, we cannot explain the observed low luminosity with the standard pre-main-sequence evolutionary track unless we assume cold accretion with an extremely small initial radius of the protostar (~0.65 R_\odot).
